Each field has this structure:

- Field Type: text / list / number / number-$ / number-percentage / date / array of ...

- **number:**

  ➤ Use 0 if not found.
- **number-$:** Monetary value starting with "$", e.g. `$50 200 000`.  
  ➤ Use space for thousands separation (every three digits).  
  ➤ No commas, dots, or other separators besides spaces and the dollar sign.  
  ➤ Leave empty "" if not found.
- **number-percentage:** Value followed by "%", e.g. `5,5%`.  
  ➤ Use comma for decimals, no rounding under any circumstances.  
  ➤ Leave empty "" if not found.
- **list:** Must match exactly one of the predefined template options. Leave empty "" if not found.
- **date:** Format as `"Month DD, YYYY"`. Leave empty "" if not found.
- **array of text:** Example: ["Value1", "Value2"]. Leave empty [] if none found.
- **array of list:** Example: ["Option1", "Option2"]. Leave empty [] if none found.
- **array of numbers:** Example: [1000, 2000]. Leave empty [] if none found.
- **array of numbers-$:** Example: ["$1 000", "$2 000"]. Leave empty [] if none found.
- **array of numbers-percentage:** Example: ["5,5%", "7%"]. Leave empty [] if none found.

**ARRAY FIELD STRUCTURE RULES:**
- Arrays **124–132**, **142–148**, **149–154**, **155–160** must maintain **index correspondence**.

  ➤ All parallel arrays in a group must have identical lengths.  
  ➤ Keep unit type consistency across related arrays.

- For arrays: include only items found in THIS chunk.  
- Do NOT assume data from other chunks.  
- Do NOT output placeholders or merged data not present in this text.

**CRITICAL PROCESSING RULES:**

107.1. number-$
107.3. Provide the dollar value for the budgeted Commercial Recovery Income per year for the Subject Property when the property is complete and stabilized that is specified in the proposed budget or development budget or proforma provided by the Borrower or the broker. Recovery Income is income received from tenants to reimburse the landlord for operating expenses such as property taxes, insurance, and maintenance, typically outlined in lease agreements.

108. Residential Vacancy Allowance, % (Borrower)
108.1. number-percentage
108.3. Provide budgeted or expected Residential Vacancy Allowance expressed as percentage points of the Potential Gross Residential Revenue for the Subject property when the property is complete and stabilized that is specified in the proposed budget or development budget or proforma provided by the Borrower or the broker. Residential Vacancy Allowance is an adjustment that accounts for expected income loss from unoccupied residential units, expressed as a percentage of potential gross rent to reflect typical market vacancy levels.

109. Commercial Vacancy Allowance, $ (Borrower)
109.1. number-$
109.3. Provide budgeted or expected Commercial Vacancy Allowance expressed as dollar amount for the Subject property when the property is complete and stabilized that is specified in the proposed budget or development budget or proforma provided by the Borrower or the broker. Commercial Vacancy Allowance is an estimated deduction from potential rental income to account for expected downtime or unleased space in commercial properties, based on prevailing market vacancy rates.

110. Operating Expenses (Borrower)
110.1. number-$
110.3. Provide the dollar value for the budgeted Operating Expenses per year for the Subject Property when the property is complete and stabilized that is specified in the proposed budget or development budget or proforma provided by the Borrower or the broker. Operating Expenses are the ongoing costs required to maintain and operate a property, including utilities, repairs, maintenance, property management, insurance, and property taxes.

111. Structural Allowance (Borrower)
111.1. number-$
111.3. Provide the dollar value for the budgeted Structural Allowance per year for the Subject Property when the property is complete and stabilized that is specified in the proposed budget or development budget or proforma provided by the Borrower or the broker. Structural Allowance is a budget provision for anticipated structural repairs or capital improvements to the building’s foundation, frame, or other load-bearing elements to ensure long-term integrity.

112. Capitalization Rate (Borrower)
112.1. number-percentage
112.3. Provide the Capitalization Rate for the Subject Property when the property is complete and stabilized that is specified in the proposed budget or development budget or proforma provided by the Borrower or the broker. As requested, and in accordance with our accepted proposal dated March 26, 2021, we completed a
geotechnical investigation of the soil conditions at the referenced site as such related to the proposed
development massing at that time. Since submitting our original report, dated June 8, 2021, the
originally contemplated single parkade level has now been increased to two levels. Therefore, this
revised report, dated July 4, 2022, supersedes our original report. Our observations and
recommendations are summarized below.

PROPOSED DEVELOPMENT

The development site combines the above noted single-family detached residential properties, with
the overall footprint bounded by similar residential properties to the east and south, a multi-family
residential property to the west, and Esquimalt Road to the north. Roughly rectangular in shape, the
combined properties encompass a total area of approximately 1,545 m’, measuring roughly 36 m
(east-west) by 43 m (north-south). The overall site is currently occupied by two residential buildings
with detached storage areas. The site location is further indicated on the attached Site Plan (Sheet 1
of 3).

Based on our recent correspondence with MTA Urban Design Architecture Design Inc., we
understand that the proposed development will now comprise a six-storey building over two levels of
underground parking. We understand that the underground parkade and parking ramp structure will
be constructed at or near the property lines. We also understand that the south foundation wall will be
offset by about 1.3 m from the southern property line and that it is desired to save several trees in this
area by minimizing the extent of the excavation. We anticipate that the parkade will consist of
reinforced concrete foundation footings and walls with a grade-supported parking level slab and that
the above-ground levels will comprise light wood-framed construction.

INVESTIGATION PROCEDURE

Our work consisted of a combination of a desktop study, site reconnaissance, and a subsurface
investigation. The desktop study included a review of quaternary geology mapping, Capital Regional
District GIS mapping, BC Water Well database, and a review of our previously completed work in
the surrounding area. Prior to ground disturbance, we contacted BC OneCall for existing utility
information at the site and we completed private utility locates at each test hole location.

On May 19, 2021, we visited the subject site to complete a site reconnaissance and subsurface
investigation. The site reconnaissance consisted of traversing the site by foot and documenting
features of significance. The subsurface investigations included the advancement of eight test holes
(TH21-01 to TH21-08) to depths up to 6.7 m below the existing ground surface. Drilling was carried
out using a track-mounted solid stem auger supplied and operated by Drillwell Enterprises Ltd. As
drilling progressed, the soils were visually identified by Ryzuk Geotechnical personnel and
representative disturbed samples were collected for subsequent laboratory testing, which was limited
to the determination of moisture content and confirmation of field identification. Test hole locations
are included with refusal depths on the attached Test-Hole Location Plan (Sheet 2 of 3). Detailed test
hole logs follow the location plan.

SURFACE AND SUBSURFACE CONDITIONS

The general topography of the site is gently sloping down to the south with an overall vertical relief
of approximately between | m to 2 m. Surface conditions generally consist of grass cover with
shrubs and trees, asphalt pathways, and asphalt surfaced parking areas with the existing buildings
occupying approximately 30% of the site area.

During the investigation, test holes were advanced to practical refusal upon glacial till, inferred
bedrock, or a possible buried concrete structure. A review of the test hole results generally revealed a
thin surficial cover of asphalt and fills underlain by a combination of soft to firm and/or stiff to very
stiff native silt with trace to some sand, trace to some clay, and trace gravel atop inferred glacial till
or bedrock. TH21-06 and TH21-08 encountered practical refusal upon inferred concrete at 0.5 m and
0.1 m below the existing site grades, respectively. The thickness of a glacial till layer can vary
significantly across a site, and as such bedrock depths across the site would be expected to vary as
well. The bedrock profile was observed to dip towards the northwest extent of the site, ranging in
depth from 1.4 m to 6.7 m below the existing ground surface across the locations drilled; however,
the bedrock surface between test hole locations is expected to be erratic, as is typical for bedrock in
the Greater Victoria region. The results of our drilling program and laboratory testing are shown on
the attached Test Hole Logs.

A static groundwater table was not noted during the investigation and long-term groundwater
monitoring is beyond the scope of this report. Groundwater was encountered in TH21-01 at an
approximate depth of 6.0 m below existing site grade. Perched water conditions within the surficial
fills should also be expected, particularly following periods of heavy and/or prolonged precipitation.
Groundwater seepage may be encountered within the glacial till layer and bedrock. It is expected that
the groundwater table will vary seasonally.

GEOTECHNICAL ASSESSMENT AND RECOMMENDATIONS

On the basis of our investigation, we consider the proposed development to be feasible from a
geotechnical perspective, albeit with the following considerations. All buried concrete/tanks and fills
associated with past/current use will need to be removed to expose suitable bearing soils/bedrock for
foundation support. Based on the subsurface soil conditions and given that two levels of underground
parking are proposed, we expect that foundations will generally bear atop bedrock; however, we
anticipate that foundations located within the northwest corner of the building may be supported by
glacial till depending on its thickness over bedrock. Where glacial till is present, we anticipate that
local slot cuts/sub-excavations could be advanced to extend footings down to bedrock (if desired).
These slot cuts/sub excavations could also be infilled back to design grade using mass concrete fill.

Given the variable bedrock profile throughout the site, and that the parkade will extend to or near the
property lines, we expect that both temporary excavation cutslopes and shoring or a combination of
both will be required. We note that it will be necessary to excavate down vertically and implement
shoring near the existing trees along the southern property line and at the northwest corner of the site.
Depending on the season when excavation is undertaken, seepage may be encountered and will
require appropriate temporary dewatering systems and disposal. Our recommendations pertaining to
temporary excavation shoring can be found in the Building Excavation and Shoring Considerations
section of this report.

Building Excavation and Shoring Considerations

Excavation and shoring requirements are highly dependent on the final building design and parkade
layout. From our recent correspondence, we anticipate excavations depths will be approximately

6 to 7 m with at or near property line construction. Where space allows, we expect that temporary
excavation cutslopes within the observed subsurface materials will be stable at the following
configurations:

Topsoil/fill materials — between 0.75H:1V and 1H:1V (Horizontal: Vertical)
Soft to Firm brown silt — between 0.75H:1V and 1H:1V

Very stiff brown silt — 0.5H:1V

Glacial Till — 0.5H: 1V

Bedrock — 0.5H: 1V to near vertical if line drilled

The stability of temporary excavation cutslopes can vary depending on the actual soil conditions
encountered, the presence of seepage, weather conditions, and the period of time they remain open.
As such, the above slope configurations may be subject to change and/or may require to be covered
with poly sheeting.

Note that all excavations deeper than 1.2 m and steeper than 0.75H:1V must be assessed by a
geotechnical professional in accordance with WorkSafeBC guidelines prior to worker entry or
approach.

Where there is insufficient room, or surface encroachment cannot be granted to accommodate the
above cutslope configurations, the use of shoring would be required. We envision that such would

consist of rock anchors with reinforced shotcrete (assuming underground encroachment is permitted)
and that vertical support members, such as micro-piles, may be locally required where the bedrock
profile is deeper. Use of shoring will also require subsurface encroachment agreements for the
underground installation of anchors across property lines. Discussions with adjacent property owners
would be required for surface and/or subsurface encroachment as previously mentioned. If
encroachment is not allowed, then the use of intermittent wall panel construction may be necessary.
Further details on these methods can be provided once encroachment options are known. We
recommend that pre-construction surveys be completed on adjacent properties prior to excavation to
establish a baseline cosmetic/structural condition. In any event, we recommend that
excavation/shoring works take place when the seasonal water table is at its lowest. This generally
occurs during the spring/summer months.

We anticipate that up to about 5 m to 6 m of rock excavation will be required below the shoring
systems to achieve the design foundation elevation(s). This would likely consist of blasting; however,
it may be possible to locally fracture bedrock using a hoe ram where the bedrock profile is close to
the foundation design grade(s). We strongly recommend line drilling the bedrock along the perimeter
of the excavation to minimize overbreak and the risk of undermining the toe of the temporary
excavation cutslopes, and shoring systems. Depending on the stability of the bedrock cutslopes, it
may be necessary to stabilize such with bolting/pinning, drapery mesh, and/or shotcrete. It will be
necessary to monitor the vibration of the surrounding areas during the excavation works. Vibration
monitoring during rock blasting should also be undertaken to ensure that peak particle velocities
(PPV) are kept below threshold values relating to adjacent structures/infrastructure. It is probable that
neighboring residents will raise concerns regarding vibrations, even if some are not structurally
harmful, and a pre-blast survey may be important to later verify or alleviate such concerns. We note
that cosmetic cracking to adjacent structures is possible.

We note that the bedrock depth/profile across the site will have a significant impact on the design and
cost of shoring and rock excavation work. A rock probing investigation could be completed to better
delineate the bedrock profile throughout the site. A proposal for this work can be provided upon
request.

Seismic Considerations

Greater Victoria is situated in a region of very high seismicity. Considerable earthquake risk exists,
stemming from its proximity to the Cascadia subduction zone and numerous more local faults in
southwestern BC and northwestern Washington State.

Given the encountered subsurface conditions and the expected design foundation elevation(s), we
anticipate that most foundations will extend down to intact bedrock. However, glacial till may be
present at the design foundation elevation within the northwest corner of the excavation. For
foundations that bear directly on bedrock or poured concrete mass fill over bedrock, it is reasonable
to expect the shear wave velocity in the upper 30 m (Vs) to be greater than 1500 m/s. This
corresponds to a Site Classification for Seismic Site Response (Site Class) of ‘A’, in accordance with
the current BC Building Code. For foundations that bear on less than three meters of glacial till
and/or engineered fill over bedrock, it is reasonable to expect the V;*° to range between 760 m/s to
1500 m/s, corresponding to a Site Class of ‘B’.

The expected transition between Site Class ‘A’ and ‘B’ is shown on the attached Seismic Site Class
Delineation (Sheet 3 of 3). It is important to note that delineation is based on test hole locations and
the respective refusals on inferred glacial till or bedrock. As such, the transition delineation between
Site Class ‘A’ and ‘B’ will need to be verified during and at the end of the excavation phase. If a Site
Class of ‘A’ is desired throughout the site, we expect that footings could be extended through the
glacial till (if present at the design foundation elevation) down to bedrock or that grade could be
recovered using mass concrete fill placed over bedrock. We note that the bedrock profile/depths
could be confirmed by conducting a rock probing investigation.

The attached 2015 National Building Code Seismic Hazard Calculation provides PGA and Spectral
Acceleration values for Site Class ‘C’ for a 2% probability of exceedance in 50 year seismic event.
These values should be corrected for Site Class ‘A’ and ‘B’ in accordance with the current BC
Building Code.

Settlements Considerations

Given the soil condition encountered during the investigation, the anticipated structure loading, and
depth of excavation, we do not foresee any significant settlement issues provided foundations are
designed in accordance with appropriate bearing resistances. However, this will need to be verified
once information regarding the anticipated structural loading and a site grading is available for
review.

Building Foundations

We expect that conventional pad and strip footings would be the preferred foundation choice. Based
on the results of the subsurface investigation and the expected design foundation elevation(s), we
expect that foundations will bear atop undisturbed glacial till, clean, intact bedrock, or mass concrete
over bedrock. These subgrades can provide long-term stable support to foundations assuming the
factored bearing resistances provided in Table 1:

Minimum footing widths of 400 and 600 mm are recommended for strip and pad footings,
respectively. Footings should be placed at least 450 mm below the final adjacent site grade to
minimize the effects of seasonal frost and/or moisture variation.

Foundation Wall Backfill & Earth Pressures

Foundation walls should be backfilled with clean, well graded granular material, with less than 5%
passing the #200 sieve. Backfill should be placed and compacted in maximum 300 mm lifts to at
least 95% of SPMDD. Additionally, adequate drainage should be provided for the backfill to prevent
the buildup of hydrostatic pressure against the foundation walls.

Foundation walls can be designed based on the attached Lateral Earth Pressure Diagrams and the
following lateral earth pressure coefficients:

Table 2. Lateral Earth Pressure Coefficients

Lateral Earth Pressure Coefficient
Wall Type Static kK Kae | AKae
Yielding (unrestrained) Active (Ka) 0.28 | 0.52 | 0.24
Non-yielding (restrained) | At-Rest(Ko) | 0.47 | - -

A yielding wall is able to move a minimum of 0.1% of the height of the wall to allow active
pressures to development. Where such movement cannot occur, the non-yielding, at-rest earth
pressure coefficient should be used. It is assumed that all walls will yield during the design seismic
event. The above earth pressure coefficients are based on a friction angle of 32 degrees (compact
sand). Lower earth pressures could be provided if better quality backfill material (well graded
crushed rock) and quality control is used during construction.

In the case where the design assumptions above and noted on the attached diagrams are not satisfied,
a site-specific assessment of the lateral earth pressures would be required. Equipment larger than a
bobcat should not be allowed within 1.5 m of the foundation walls during backfilling.

Engineered Fill

Where it will be necessary to raise grades back to design grade in over-excavated areas, engineered
fill would be required. Engineered fill is to consist of select granular material (such as 75 mm minus
crushed rock or smaller) at or near optimum moisture content. Engineered fill is to be placed on
approved subgrade under the supervision of a geotechnical professional, in maximum 300 mm lifts
and compacted to a minimum of 95% of Standard Proctor Maximum Dry Density (SPMDD) or
judged equivalent. The engineered fill must have a footprint that extends horizontally beyond the
footings a distance equal to the thickness of the engineered fill, to provide adequate splay for
foundation loads. If adequate space to achieve loading splay is not available along perimeter areas,
lowering the foundations could be considered.

Grade Supported Parkade Slab

We consider the use of a reinforced concrete slab on grade to be feasible. For the parkade level slab,
we recommend that a poly vapor barrier and a minimum of 150 mm of well-graded 19 mm (-)
crushed rock be placed directly beneath the slab in order to provide uniform support and prevent
capillary action on the underside of the slab. All sub slab fills should be compacted to at least 95% of
SPMDD value or judged equivalent by a qualified geotechnical professional. In areas where the sub-
slab soil consists of glacial till or where seasonal groundwater levels may rise to near base of slab
elevation, sub-slab interior drains are recommended (as described in the drainage section).

Drainage Considerations

As noted previously, a static groundwater table was not noted during the subsurface investigation;
however, perched groundwater conditions should be anticipated. Regardless, short term temporary
dewatering during construction will likely be accommodated by conventional sump and pump

arrangements. Historical groundwater table often taken to be at/near transition between brown and

grey clay.

We would consider a conventional perimeter foundation drainage system suitable to prevent the
buildup of hydrostatic pressure against the foundation walls. The foundation drain arrangement
(perforated pipe and uniform gravel/drain rock) should be covered with non-woven geotextile filter
fabric (not landscape fabric), or a suitably graded granular medium, to prevent migration of finer
materials from the backfill into voids within the drain arrangement. Additionally, the drainage system
should be directly/hydraulically connected to the recommended free draining backfill material. This,
however, does not preclude the possibility of dampness and/or minor seepage, which would be
considered building envelope concerns.

Where perimeter drains will be located on the inside of the building, weep holes should be provided
in the foundation wall with clear drain rock providing hydraulic connectivity between the free
draining exterior backfill and/or drainage mat, and the perforated drain. Where foundation walls are
to be constructed near or against property boundaries, perimeter drainage can be placed on the inside
of the foundation wall with drainage from the outside face established using drainage board and weep
holes of 100 mm diameter spaced every 2 m. Allowance should be made for placement of additional
interior drainage as necessary to accommodate any localized zones of seepage that may be
encountered during construction works. Plumbing and building envelope details will be by others.

Any foundation elements, slab on grades, pits or elevator shafts that are not effectively drained to the
perimeter drains will require their own drainage arrangement or will need to be designed to resist
hydrostatic pressures.

Note that it is not the intent of the perimeter wall backfill to accommodate storm water flow. Storm
water must be collected in a separate system for remote discharge.

Further to the Architects Act and Bylaws 28 and 29, the AIBC Council has endorsed an amended approach
with regard to both the recommended net architectural percentage fees and the scope of basic architectural
services in the “Market Multiple-Residential Sector”. This approach represents a professionally
supportable departure from the familiar, traditional “Basic Services” package in Appendix I of the AIBC
Tariff and carries with that a corresponding, more flexible, sliding scale of recommended fees. It was
developed under the auspices of the AIBC’s Fees and Services Committee, within the Practice Board.

The chief amendments relative to Appendix I’s Basic Services are, broadly: (1) Add: services respecting
one cycle of zoning/development permit applications across the schematic and design development phases;
(2) Delete: bidding and negotiation phase services; (3) Delete: cost estimating in all phases; and (4) Delete:
construction contract administration and payment certification.

proposals of services-and-fees and new agreements are expected to be in substantial compliance with the

Summary of Approach to the “Market-Multiple Residential Sector” Tariff

These results stem from the research and findings of a working group (representing 14 architectural firms)
that met over the past two years with the objective of updating the Tariff of Fees for Architectural Services
for new construction in the Market Multiple Residential Sector. Market Multiple Residential renovations
were not considered. The phrase “market” suggests a developer-initiated project not involving public
agency participation. Usually in this sector, the terms of the contractual relationship between the owner
and the builder, who in most cases is (effectively) the same party, are neither disclosed to, nor administered
by the architect. Projects characterized as being non-market, or congregate care, were outside the scope of
this review and its recommendations.

Part of the approach was to develop some empirical data to ascertain what are the current acceptable fees
for services in this sector. Members of the working group prepared proposals for a number of hypothetical
projects based on the number of hours it would take to do the projects. This was a form of cost-check and
the catalyst to clarify the basic assumptions underlying the services provided.

Cross-reference was made to the chart of services (Sequence and Scope) on the last page of the current
Tariff. There are black dots beside some of the services that denote “basic” and therefore are covered by
the Tariffs percentage-fee recommendations. The origin of this list is the research and development work
of the first (1986) Tariff, monitored and updated since, and kept consistent with standard client-architect
agreements, construction contracts and building regulations. The consensus is that the chart has become
somewhat out of step with what is currently the practice in this sector. The enclosed modified list of Basic
Services was developed and endorsed for this sector.

It is notable that in this sector, contrary to the current standard basic services in the Tariff and NPP Client-
Architect Agreement, Document 6, one cycle of the rezoning and development permit process is commonly
included in basic services. On the other hand, tendering is not usually included, and neither are any
services related to progress certificates or quantification of the value of the work. While it is recognized
that the architect needs to approve changes to the work, and to be aware of relevant communications, the
change order procedure does not necessarily require the organizational framework, in this case, as it does
for other sectors.

A review of construction documents was done and a list of necessary Construction Documents (including
working drawings and specifications) was developed. Since tendering and contract administration are not
included in basic services, the specifications in this sector consist mostly of products, performance
standards, assembly illustrations and schedules to satisfy code compliance (i.e. the so-called “technical”
and quality assurance aspects).

The number of variables to consider in providing services during construction makes it extremely difficult
to be precise about the fees. The reviews generically identified in the current Tariffs Basic Services chart
were expanded and a sequential checklist of field reviews was prepared.

To translate the estimated hours for our hypothetical sample projects into a fee an hourly rate of $85.00 was
used. This was assumed to be a blended rate. It was noted that the beginning and ending of the project

take more “principal’s” time than do the intermediate phases.

BACKGROUND

The proposed project in Victoria is comprised of Esquimalt consists of a six-storey, wood frame
residential rental building of approx. 33,955 SF with approx. 59 units and a 1.5 level

The envelope assemblies are not clear from the drawings, we assume the exterior walls will be
clad with a conventional cladding system. Glazing systems will be a residential assembly.

Below grade conditions are not confirmed but considering the neighbouring properties we
have assumed that there will be no hydrostatic pressure.

addresses energy modelling and energy consulting services for Step Code and BCBC. No
additional sustainability measures are being sought. The overarching goal is to have an

DISCUSSION, CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
ANTICIPATED TREE REMOVALS AND MITIGATION MEASURES

Construction of the new six-plex building will result in the loss of 6 protected trees: the four
protected Leyland cypress trees in the group of five growing along the property boundary with
the neighbour to the east, and three of four municipal boulevard trees fronting the site and in the
median of Esquimalt Road.

Leyland cypress “boundary” trees:

Large surficial roots from the Leyland cypress trees are cracking and heaving the adjacent
asphalt driveway access into existing Lot 861. The crowns of the trees extend well into the
proposed building footprint and are not amenable to crown reduction pruning of the magnitude
required. The distance from the base of the trees to the edge of the building excavation,
assuming vertical shoring, is only 1.6 m, which is inside of the critical root plate radius and close
to the zone of rapid root taper. Excavation this close to the trees will destabilize the trees, with
the likelihood of failure and impact very likely with consequences ranging from significant to
severe, depending upon which of several high-value targets are struck.? For these reasons, all
five of these trees are recommended for removal and replacement.

A tree growing across property boundaries is considered in law to be “held in common” between
the two property owners; as such, the consent of both owners is required if the removal of a
boundary tree is desired. Prior to rezoning or a development permit being granted, the
Township of Esquimalt will require written authorization from the co-owner of the Leyland
cypress trees for their removal. Further, the Township's tree bylaw requires that replacement
trees be planted on the same property from which the associated trees were removed. In this
instance, nine replacement trees are required to mitigate the loss of the four protected cypress
specimens, but it is unclear on which property the replacement trees should be planted.

Assuming permission for the tree removals is obtained, it is recommended that the replacement
trees be divided more or less evenly between the two properties.

Municipal trees:

Road frontage improvements and site servicing will necessitate the removal of two municipal
trees (M-1 and M-4): one magnolia growing on the fronting boulevard that conflicts with the
proposed parkade entrance and one maple growing in the street median that conflicts with
changes to the traffic pattern associated with the development.

RETAINED TREES AND PROTECTION MEASURES

Two municipal boulevard tree (M-1) is proposed for retention and protection. Arborist
supervision shall be provided for all frontage works undertaken by the applicant within or
adjacent to the protected root zone of this tree. Tree protection fencing and caution-
signage shall be erected to the satisfaction of the Township, as indicated on the attached
plan, prior to site work commencing.

dramatically reduce any potential impacts arising from the proposed development to these
trees.

Tree protection fencing and caution-signage will be emplaced to prevent any encroachment
into the sensitive area between the proposed south parkade wall and the existing retaining
wall without the presence of the project arborist.

Excavation for the parkade along the south side shall be supervised by the project arborist.

In addition to the above, at the recommendation of the project arborist, the south parkade
wall has been shifted north by 1.3 m away from the wall and trees. Care is required to
safely excavate the foundation of the parkade along this wall, while minimizing
encroachment toward the retaining wall. The depth of soil to bedrock is considered to be 3
— 4m at the south end of the site. Backsloping will be required to safely attack the bedrock
beneath. Shotcrete and soil nailing may also be required. The bedrock will be line-drilled.
Alternate rock removal techniques will be employed where possible. Where blasting is
required, best practices will be deployed to minimize impacts to the existing retaining wall
that the off-site trees adjacent to it, including the following:
¢ Apre-construction meeting between the general contractor, rock removal contractor
and the project arborist to develop a least-impactful rock removal work plan;
« — Line-drilling to minimize overbreakage,
« Use of dynamite in place of ammonium nitrate (less toxic to tree roots),
« Creation of a relief zone for the blast wave away from the retaining wall and trees,
«  Adrilling and blasting plan that uses smaller charges and minimizes peak particle
velocity,
« “Decking” of explosive charges to sequence the demolition of the charge,
« Deployment of seismometers to measure and record peak particle velocity along
the sensitive areas.

Assembled, the Subject site is rectangular shaped and has sole frontage of +127 feet along
Esquimalt Road. The site is relatively level throughout with a slight sloping in a southern
direction away from its adjoining roadway. The site is currently improved with two residential
structures; however, is assumed to be vacant with no contributory value to its existing
improvements. It has no unusual topography noted. According to the site plan provided by the

or site bearing capacity issues.

is likely the next phase in this area's evolution.

10.0 HIGHEST AND BEST USE

As stated in the 2024 report on Canadian Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal
(CUSPAP), published by the Appraisal Institute of Canada’s Standards Committee, Highest and
Best use can be defined as:

"The reasonably probable use of real property, that is physically possible, legally
permissible, financially feasible and maximally productive, and that results in the
highest value."

It is to be recognized that in cases where a site has existing improvements on it, the highest
and best use may very well be determined to be different from the existing use. The existing
use will continue, however, unless and until land value in its highest and best use exceeds the
total value of the property in its existing use.

The four criteria the highest and best use must meet are physical possibility, legal permissibility,
financial feasibility and maximum productivity. Implied within these criteria is recognition of the
contribution of that specific use to community environment or to community development goals
in addition to wealth maximisation of individual property owners. As such, the latter two criteria
are jointly addressed under a more general economically feasible subheading.

11.0 METHOD OF VALUATION

The appraisal process involves a systematic analysis of the factors that bear upon the value of
real estate. In estimating the Market Values of the Subject Property as of the effective date,
November 28, 2024 the following conventional methods of appraisal have been considered.

The Cost Approach

The Cost Approach to value assumes that a prudent purchaser will not pay more for a property
than the cost to recreate it in its present condition provided there are no costly delays or
economic factors which might influence value. The approach involves the determination of the
replacement cost of the improvements, less depreciation, plus the value of the land, as though
vacant.

The Direct Comparison Approach

This approach to value is based on the Principle of Substitution, which affirms that a prudent
purchaser will not pay more for a property than the price of an equally desirable substitute
property available under similar conditions. This approach provides a reliable indication of
value, particularly in an active market, given a reasonable availability of market data having a
sufficient degree of comparability to the Subject.

The Income Approach

The Income Approach involves a conversion of anticipated future benefits to be derived from
the ownership of property into a value estimate through a capitalization process, which converts
the anticipated future income and/or reversions to a present worth estimate. Within the Income
Approach, the two methods, which are conventionally used, are the Direct Capitalization
Method and the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) Method.

=== Page 49 ===
Selected Methodologies

The Subject Property will be an income producing property whereby the cash flow is
quantifiable. The Cost Approach is typically used to determine value for purposes such as
insurance, special purpose buildings and new projects. However, the Cost Approach does not
recognize its income generating capability for which this type of asset typically trades; therefore,
the Cost Approach has been excluded for purposes of this appraisal.

The Development Approach, which is a derivative of the Cost Approach, was applied to
estimate the “As Is” Land value of the Subject. The Development Approach allows an appraiser
to determine the residual land value of a site based on market sales data and development cost
estimates. This approach applies the overall potential sale value of the proposed development
as a starting point. The associated development costs are then applied against the net proceeds

11.3 INCOME APPROACH - “As If Complete & Occupied”

The Income Approach is based on the belief that income-producing properties are purchased
as an investment; therefore, the assumption is that the investor measures the value of the
property based on its income generating capability. Hence, all things being equal, the higher
the income, the higher the value, as the income is capitalized into value by an appropriate rate.
The Income Approach can be capitalized into value by either selection of an appropriate cap.
rate or multiplier.

As previously discussed, within the Income Approach there are two Methods of valuation: the
Discounted Cash Flow Method and the Direct Capitalization Method. The former is useful for
more complicated commercial properties that are subject to frequent fluctuations in their
revenues and expenses. It involves forecasting over a period of time, usually 5 to 10 years,
with the resulting income present valued and summarized into a final estimate of value. The
Direct Capitalization Method is considered to be a “snapshot” of a property’s revenue and
expenses whereas the Discounted Cash Flow Method is considered more of a “moving picture”.
For purposes of this analysis, the Direct Capitalization Method was applied, which best reflects
how this type of investment is typically traded.

Direct Capitalization Method

This approach utilizes an analysis whereby the Potential Net Operating Income is stabilized for
a 12 month period. This stabilized NOI is then converted into value based on a market derived
capitalization rate. In stabilizing the Subject’s NOI as of the effective date, several primary and
secondary information sources were reviewed. Rent rolls and income statements available from
comparable properties were reviewed to establish appropriate gross potential rental revenue
as well as expense ratios and ranges. In addition, interviews were conducted with property
managers and owners to further support the Subject’s stabilized net operating income analysis.
Market data, including CMHC reports, were reviewed in order to establish norms and trends for
revenues and expenses.

The Subject has yet to be completed and/or occupied; therefore, historical revenues and
expenses do not exist. When complete, there will be 59 units within a 6 storey rental building.
The building will feature a variety of layouts ranging from Bachelor to three bedroom units with
one live work unit on the ground floor. All residential suites will feature in suite laundry and an
exterior area with the exception of bachelor units. All units are assumed to be available for
market rental with no rental covenants or restrictions for purposes of the Direct Capitalization
Method.

Capitalization Rate Selection

An income rate is the relationship between income aspects of a property and its current market
value. Several types of capitalization rates or multipliers exist, however the most commonly
accepted and applied are: The Overall Capitalization Rate, Gross Income/Rent Multiplier and
the Equity Capitalization (dividend) Rate. In this instance, the Overall Capitalization Rate will be
applied and relied upon.

Capitalization rates, which are derived from sales of comparable properties, is most commonly
used amongst practitioners, as it is the most direct method and is easily quantifiable. The
appraiser analyzes sales of comparable properties, which have similar investments features,
expense ratios, financing, ages, property type, etc. Stabilization of the income and expenses
to obtain the NOI must be performed on all properties including the Subject Property in a similar
manner. Aspects such as a Structural Allowance must be consistently applied among the
comparables as well as to the Subject.

of roughly +2 years. The Client's budget indicates a total financing cost of $2,420,000 which
includes an Interest Reserve of $2,100,000 plus Broker and Lenders’ Fees of $320,000, or
$160,000 each respectively. This appears reasonable compared to other budgets and
consideration of the current lending climate with high borrowing costs and is applied herein.
This appropriately reflects the higher risk related to financing at this time and would not require
further contingency to be applied.

Combined the soft costs equate to roughly 22.74% of hard costs, which is in line with expected
ratios between 20.0% and 30.0%.

Construction/Development Management Fee

A development management fee based on the Client’s proposed $835,000 estimate is applied
herein. This equates to +3.75% of total costs excluding land costs. This is in line with expected
development management fees which can be as low as 3.0% and as high as 5.0%. It is noted
that a lower management fee is itemized in the Client's proforma at $400,000. In discussions
with the Client it only reflects a partial management fee due to internal agreements between the
development group.

It is assumed that construction management fee is including in the hard cost budget; however
no detailed hard cost line item budget was available.

Contingency Allowance

The Subject’s hard costs and soft costs are expressed excluding contingency allowance. In
recent years there have been notable supply issues for both labour and construction materials
which have impacted construction costs. Construction costs and the industry as a whole are
still recovering from elevated levels with some reports of more flattened or stable costs at this
time. That being said, there is still risk and uncertainty from suppliers and the labour market,
which will require some buffer and contingency to be considered by any prudent developer.

Total hard costs including management and construction costs total roughly $325.00 psf and
+$420.00 including its underground parking component, which is in line, albeit the higher end
of expected costs.

The Client’s provided budget includes a contingency allowance that is based on percentage of
hard and soft costs that equate to a blended rate just above 5.0%. For purposes of this analysis
an average contingency allowance of 10.0% on total costs in addition to the development

GST Self — Assessment

The Government of Canada is providing a 100% rebate of GST on new purpose-built rental
housing for projects of 4 units ore more that are held for long term rental. Construction must
commence after September 13, 2023 but before 2031 and must be substantially completed
before 2036. Therefore, the proposed development should be exempt from the GST self-
assessment cost.

Developer's Profit

Unlike retail condo buildings, rental buildings are primarily built for the potential cash flow return
on the investment and equity. Simply they are viewed more as a long term holding property that
will provide annual return on investment and/or equity. A typical Developer’s profit is not
expected int his case as a purpose built rental building ahs differing investment parameters than
a retail condo project. In the former, the benefit to the developer would be the ongoing cash
flow, in perpetuity. In the latter, the value would be in the net sales profit. As such a purpose
built rental building’s market value would not share a similar spread between total cost and
gross sell out value. Hence no additional profit margins other than those built in for construction
management and development management.

11.5 DIRECT COMPARISON APPROACH - Development Land Value

The Direct Comparison Approach relies on sales data of comparable properties in order to
estimate the Market Value of a Subject Property. In essence it “looks at the differences in the
legal, physical, locational and economic characteristics of comparable sales and listings, and
more closely on differences in the property rights, the sale dates, the listing dates, the motivation
of the parties and the financing.“ The Direct Comparison Approach is based on several
appraisal principles with the principle of substitution being the most relevant to the Approach.
Therefore, the Direct Comparison Approach relies on the availability and comparability of
existing sales evidence.

This Subject Property reflects materially rezoned development land; therefore, other land sales
that are zoned to permit their intended development will be the best indicator of market value
for the Subject. Sites that are zoned for low to medium density developments including
traditional townhouse, stacked townhouse and condo/apartment or any combination of these
layouts are considered herein

This is the process of comparing market data; that is, the prices paid for similar properties
bought and sold in the open market. This approach is based upon the principle of substitution,
which infers that a prudent purchaser would pay no more for a property than it would cost to
purchase an equally desirable substitute property.

The Subject’s Land Value is based on the proposed purpose built rental development. The
following sales are believed to be some of the most recent sales of development sites, which
are similar to the Subject Property. It is noted that sales from across the Region were included;
however with a focus on the Subject market of Esquimalt as well as Victoria and Saanich. In
saying this, it is noted that Esquimalt’s calculation / interpretation of FSR/FAR differs from these
other municipalities in that they do not include the common areas, amenities, and areas that
are used by all residents such as hallways, corridors etc. This effectively would increase the
actual FAR based on gross building area by roughly +15.0% on most Esquimalt lands given
that is a typical efficiency level. For the Subject, the efficiency is slightly lower with just under
80% net livable area versus gross floor area. As such, it is best to try and standardize the gross
building area to a similar interpretation of FAR for purposes of this analysis.

The Subject’s gross floor area of 42,530 square feet (excludes parking and rooftop) is
considered herein. In addition, the Esquimalt sales are adjusted based on an average of 85.0%
efficiency level to better compare the data to the non-Esquimalt land sales.

will not require rezoning. This has a similar, yet lower permitted achievable FSR at 1.50 to the
Subject. That being said, given its superior location and lower density yield this is considered
to be well above the Subject’s achievable pbsf value at $120.00. If adjusted, this would support
a value below $100 pbsf.

things being equal. These are in high traffic neighbourhoods with a similar mix of residential
and commercial uses in the immediate area. It did require rezoning to allow for a higher density
residential development. The location adjustment would be offset by rezoning adjustment.

Index #4, 790 Wilson Street & 802 Hereward Road reflects the sale of two improved
properties with the improvements considered to be of limited contributory value. This is located
nearby in Vic West; however, this is considered an inferior location relative to the Subject that
is adjacent to an industrial park. This is a smaller sized site with a much lower density yield;
however, warranted adjustments would be more than offset by the Subject’s superior zoning
and location. This site has a much lower density and plans are for townhouse site versus
multifamily. It was included given it is a recent sale and located in a comparable location but
given little to no weight.

The Cost Approach is best used for new buildings; however, it does not consider the income
generating capacity of the investment. A derivative of this approach was relied upon to
determine the land value. This was a secondary guide to value along with the Direct Comparison
Approach estimate of the As Is development land value.

The Direct Comparison Approach focuses on the physical characteristics of the asset, as
opposed to its financial composition. It is generally less popular amongst market participants
than the Income Approach. This has been given secondary weight to the Income Approach for
the As If Complete and Occupied market value. This approach was also applied to estimate the
As ls Development land value in addition to the Development Approach.

The Income Approach is relatively well founded on recent market evidence from the general
area. It measures one of the key elements of return on investment - the potential income stream,
and it is popular amongst market participants. It is noted that the Subject’s income is
quantifiable; therefore, this approach is considered reliable for the As If Complete and Occupied
market valuation.

BC Hydro Duct Settlement Commentary

As requested, we write to provide commentary relating to the stability of the ground available for support of the new BC
Hydro conduit at the following site location:

e Conduit entering at northwest comer of the parkade from PMT to Parkade Level 1 Electrical Room

The conduit will access the building through the new parkade perimeter foundation wall. Conventional excavation and
construction techniques will create a narrow zone of backfill against the outside of the perimeter foundation wall. The
conduit is expected to pass through near surface mineral soil then across the granular backfill zone and enter through
the reinforced concrete parkade wall.

Competent bearing soils/rock for foundation support are expected. Accordingly negligible foundation settlement is
expected. Provided the foundation wall backfill is selected, placed, and compacted in accordance with good building
practice, there will be negligible settlement attributable to post construction densification of the backfill material. The
surrounding mineral soil is expected to consist of a very stiff brown sandy silt, capable of supporting a well bedded
conduit.

Accordingly, and given the above, we consider that there is negligible risk of differential settlement impacting the service
ducts for the lifetime of the installation.

During construction activities, we recommend that Ryzuk Geotechnical be contacted in order to specifically monitor the
selection, placement, and compaction of the perimeter wall backfill in this area.

We trust that the preceding is suitable for your purposes at present. If you have any questions, please call. We
appreciate the opportunity to be of service to you.

Executive Summary

Loan Request

Request for first mortgage high-leverage construction financing in the amount of $23,130,000 (85% LTC) to
support the development of a 59-unit apartment project in Esquimalt, BC. Municipal council awarded 3 reading
to the subject property on November 4, 2024, with the Development Permit application submitted thereafter.
The project is expected to break ground in June of this year and the sponsor is currently going through a detailed
tender of costs and building permit submission.

Purpose

This construction financing will be refinanced upon project completion with CMHC-insured financing through the
MLI Select program or the sale of the asset. This approach enables the Borrower flexibility to finance / sell based
on rental rates at the time of completion. i.e. the sponsor would be able to secure CMHC financing at the market
rate at the time of project delivery instead of anchoring to lower rental rates today.

Current financing on the two lots is $2,100,000 with a 1-year term at a floating rate. The request is to provide a
construction loan with a land advance to replace the existing loans, and commence construction, with the 59-unit
project expected to be completed in 24-months from funding.

Subject Lands and Project

The subject lands consist of 16,627 sf (0.38 acres), with frontage along Esquimalt Road and are currently
improved with two residential structures, which are slated for demolition prior to the first construction advance.
The site received third reading approval for rezoning to CD No. 158 (Comprehensive Development) with no
objections.

Upon completion, Crestview - the subject property, will comprise a 59-unit, six-story wood-framed apartment
building atop two levels of underground parking. The first parking level will be partially at grade with the first
floor, resulting in a partial main floor. This level will house the main lobby/entrance, as well as an amenity/social
room equipped with a kitchen and washroom. The units will range in size from 418 to 923 sf, with an average size
of 568 sf. All suites will feature air conditioning and modern finishes. At grade, the subject will include outdoor
amenity space including green space, an outdoor patio dining / common area with barbeques. The building
offers a net rentable area of 33,500 sf and a gross buildable area of 43,235 sf.

Greater Victoria

Located on the southern extremity of Vancouver Island, the Capital Region of Greater Victoria comprises a total
area of nearly 2,400 square kilometres and is comprised of 13 incorporated municipalities and 3 unincorporated
electoral areas. The region stretches from Saturna Island on the east, takes in Greater Victoria and the Saanich
Peninsula, and includes that part of Vancouver Island lying south of the Malahat Mountain range and east of Port
Renfrew. The City of Victoria is geographically small at the southernmost tip of the Capital Region and has the
highest density of all 13 municipalities.

Overall, Victoria has historically been considered a desirable location in terms of natural features and overall
lifestyle with a high proportion of retirees; however, wages and well-paid job opportunities have been limited

especially for the younger demographic compared to larger cities such as Vancouver and Toronto. The increased

Town of Esquimalt

The Town of Esquimalt occupies the central portion of a large peninsula, west of the City of Victoria, on the south
end of Vancouver Island. Incorporated in 1912, it has an area of 7.08 square kilometres and a population of
17,533 (Based on 2021 Census Statistics). Esquimalt shares the peninsula with Victoria West, a mostly residential
suburb of the City of Victoria, on the east, and View Royal, a small mainly residential area. It is bound by the
Gorge Waterway to the north and by Victoria and Esquimalt Harbour to the south.

The majority of residential development in Esquimalt is characterized by single family homes and medium
density multi-family apartment buildings. It has historically been known as a lower income neighbourhood with
older stock, apart from the area surrounding the various waterways. In recent years, Esquimalt has increasingly
become home to mid end single family homes and mid end apartment buildings. This is in part due to being
more affordable compared to the neighbouring City of Victoria. Overall, the neighbourhood is in a transitional
stage from lower income to a more desirable area for commercial and residential use, with an improving rental
stock and good proximity to most amenities. New development along the waterfront has improved Esquimalt
and surrounding areas; however, the Esquimalt core and non-waterfront areas are still associated with older
inventory and low to middle income residents. Gentrification is likely the next phase in this area's evolution.

Highlights from CMHC's Fall 2024 Rental Market Report (Victoria)

The overall vacancy rate reached its highest level since 2013 while vacancies remained low in the city
centre.

The overall vacancy rate increased to 2.6% with significant increases in Langford/View Royal/Colwood (Zone 7)
while remaining low in the City of Victoria (Table 1.1.1). In Langford, a 24.8% increase in the purpose-built rental
universe pushed vacancy rates up. New units outside of the city centre tend to have longer lease-up times, which
likely drove the increase.

Supported by a substantial government sector, the labour market remains resilient with low unemployment
unlike nearby major markets like Vancouver, Calgary and Edmonton. This bolstered rental demand in Victoria.

Students drive rental demand in the Saanich and Oak Bay areas near the University of Victoria. Vacancy rates in
both zones were well below the CMA average as rental supply has not kept up with demand historically. The
number of units under construction in Saanich roughly doubled from 2023 to 2024, signaling more rental supply
growth in the next 12 to 24 months.

High demand pushed rent growth, worsening affordability

An_influx_of new rental units contributed to increases in average rents especially in Langford. Rents for 2-
bedroom units in Victoria surpassed those of Toronto, making Victoria the second most expensive market _in
Canada, behind Vancouver

Same-sample average 2-bedroom rent growth declined to 3.6% in 2024 (Table 1.1.5). A substantial increase in
supply and the higher vacancy rates contributed to slower rent growth despite strong demand.

Turnover remained above the CMA average in the Langford and Sidney areas. Renters living in these areas are
likely to be renting at a rate closer to market rents and have fewer incentives to stay in place. Meanwhile,
turnover rates declined in the City of Victoria, reflecting tighter market conditions.

Purpose-built rental growth accelerated especially in Langford

added in the area stretching from Langford to Sooke accounted for over half of the increase, while units added in
the city accounted for less than one third.

Victoria

economic contributor, generating significant activity in the marine and defence industries. Businesses
within Esquimalt Harbour alone contribute $2.4 billion annually to the regional economy, supporting
thousands of jobs and local commerce.

Population and Median Age: Victoria's population, as of the 2021 Census, is 91,867, with a median age of
42.8 years. This is slightly older than the national median age of 41.6. Victoria is known to be a quiet and
family-oriented location, home to many students, families and seniors. Employment rate in 2021 was
61.7%, with an 8.1% unemployment.

Labour Market and Economic Composition: The city's economy is driven by public administration, health
care, and education, sectors that are supported by being the provincial capital. Government jobs
constitute a large percentage of employment, alongside a growing technology sector contributing over $4
billion annually to the regional economy. Median household income is $67,500.

Housing and Living Costs: Victoria has one of Canada's highest housing costs, with the 2023 benchmark
price for a single-family home sitting around $1.25 million. This, combined with limited rental vacancy
rates (under 3%), highlights ongoing housing affordability challenges.

University of Victoria's Regional Role: The University of Victoria (UVic) enrols over 22,000 students and
contributes $1.8 billion annually to the local economy. UVic supports thousands of direct and indirect
jobs, including in research, technology, and spin-off businesses that benefit the broader Vancouver Island
region.

DEFINITIONS

The following Definitions apply to this Contract Documents. References in the definition to the singular shall be considered to
include the plural as the context requires.

Class A Construction Cost Estimate

The Class A Construction Cost Estimate is an estimate of the Construction Cost based on the completed Contract Documents.
Class A Construction Cost Estimate is the final estimate before the bid or proposal call Class A Construction Cost Estimate
shall be presented in elemental format and include labour and material costs, allowance for all costs resulting from the Project
schedule, all actual associated costs, including cash allowances, contingencies, allowances for design, escalation, market
conditions and anticipated amendment amounts as applicable.

Class B Construction Cost Estimate

The Class B Construction Cost Estimate is an estimate of the Construction Cost with a level of precision that is based on the
degree of completion of the Contract Documents at the time of preparation of the estimate. The Class B Construction Cost
Estimate is typically prepared when all site or installation investigations are completed and the design of the major systems and
sub-systems of the Project (including outline specifications and preliminary drawings and models) are well underway. Class
B Construction Cost Estimate shall be presented in elemental format and include labour and material costs, allowance for all
costs resulting from the Project schedule, all actual associated costs, including cash allowances, contingencies, allowances for
design, escalation, market conditions and anticipated amendment amounts as applicable.

Class C Construction Cost Estimate

The Class C Construction Cost Estimate is an estimate of the Construction Cost based on updated Owner requirements,
general description of the Project, preliminary site information and existing conditions, and takes into consideration market
conditions as well as basic implementation logistics. Class C Construction Cost Estimate shall include labour and material
costs and the Owner’s construction contingencies and allowances.

Class D Construction Cost Estimate

The Class D Construction Cost Estimate is an estimate of the Construction Cost based on the Owner’s functional requirements
to the degree known at the time. The Class D Construction Cost Estimate shall as a minimum be based on historical cost data
for similar projects, suitably adjusted for such factors as inflation, location, risk, quality, size, and time. All related factors
affecting cost are considered to the extent possible. The Class D Construction Cost Estimate provides the Owner an indication
of the order of magnitude of the Construction Cost for a project completed within the estimated completion date, and shall
include labour and material costs and the Owner's construction contingencies and allowances.

Change Directive

A Change Directive is a written instruction prepared by the Consultant and signed by the Owner directing the Construction
Manager to proceed with a change in the Work within the general scope of this Contract prior to the Owner and the
Construction Manager agreeing upon an adjustment in any or all of the Construction Manager’s Fee, the Guaranteed
Maximum Price and the Contract Time.

Change Order
A Change Order is a written amendment to this Contract prepared by the Consultant and signed by the Owner and the
Construction Manager stating their agreement upon:

a change in the Services;

- achange in the Work;

- the method of adjustment or the amount of the adjustment in the Construction Manager's Fee, if any;

the method of adjustment or the amount of the adjustment in the Guaranteed Maximum Price, if any;

- the extent of the adjustment in the Contract Time, if any; and

the options described in Article A-8 of the Agreement - OPTIONS.

Construction Cost

Construction Cost means the actual cost of all elements of the Project including all applicable taxes but excluding the
applicable value added taxes, whether recoverable or not. Construction Cost does not include the Construction Manager’s
Fee, the reimbursable expenses for the Services as described in Article A-6 of the Agreement — REIMBURSABLE
EXPENSES FOR THE SERVICES and the compensation of the Consultant.

Construction Cost Estimate

Construction Cost Estimate is either a Class A Construction Cost Estimate, a Class B Construction Cost Estimate, a Class C
Construction Cost Estimate, or a Class D Construction Cost Estimate, as the context shall require and is prepared with a level
of precision commensurate with the level of detail of information available at the time.

When determining applicable water use, a 500-metre radius of the Site is examined for the

applicable. Similarly, there is no groundwater use for livestock or irrigation within 500 metres of

3.2.1. Water Use Determination — Current and Future

In accordance with CSR Protocol 21, site-specific information is required to determine the
applicability of current and future drinking water use at a site. Current drinking water use applies
where there is knowledge that groundwater is being used for drinking water. Based on a search
of the BC Water Resources Atlas, there are no known water wells located within a 500 metre
radius of the Site; therefore, groundwater does not currently appear to be used for drinking water
purposes.

However, by default, future drinking water use applies to all drinking water aquifers below a site,
regardless of whether they are currently being used for this purpose. The Wark-Colquitz Aquifer
(Aquifer number 680) underlies the Site. The aquifer is a partially confined bedrock aquifer and
confinement is provided by overlying clay and till sediments. There are no known shallow drinking
water aquifers within the Site area.

4.4 Groundwater Investigation

The sections below outline the methodology used for the groundwater investigation.

4.4.1 Monitoring Well Installation

BH19-2 was completed as groundwater monitoring well. The location of the well was based on
the proximity of APEC2 identified in the Stage 1 PSI and can be referenced in Figure 4.

The well was constructed with washed and wrapped 50 mm (2") diameter, schedule 80, flush-
threaded PVC. Slotted screen casings were installed at the bottom of the hole, with a maximum
length of 1.5 metres (5’). Solid PVC blank casings were used for the remaining upper portion of
the hole. The base of the monitoring well was plugged with a PVC, threaded cap. The space
surrounding each screened length was backfilled with clean silica filter sand, from the base of the
well to 0.3 metres (1') above the screened section. A minimum of 0.5 metres of hydrated bentonite
chips was added, creating a bentonite seal to prevent infiltration from the surface. The monitoring
well was capped with a 50 mm (2") J-plug and covered with a cemented, steel, flush-mounted
road box. The wells was installed in the borehole at 3.1 m bgs. Well completion details are
included on the borehole logs, which can be referenced in Appendix B.

4.4.2 Monitoring Well Development

The well was developed to remove drilling debris and fine solids from the well screen and filter
zone surrounding the screen. If a well is not developed, the drilling debris and fine particles may
influence the water level response time, hydraulic conductivity estimates, and groundwater quality
samples. A standard-capacity Waterra inertial pumping system activated by a Waterra Hydrolift
was used for well development. A 1.6 cm outer diameter HDPE Waterra tubing was fitted with a
surge block and foot valve. Starting at the bottom of the screen, the foot valve/surge block was
placed at successively shallower locations until the top of the screen was reached so that the
entire screened zone was developed. Development at each interval continued until diminishing
sediment returns had been reached and the extracted water was relatively clear. The surge block
was then removed, the foot valve was placed at the top of the screen, and pumping was resumed.
Water volume, sediment quantity, pH, and electrical conductivity were recorded. Lastly, the foot

6.0 RESULTS
6.1 Field Observations

The geological conditions of the subsurface were observed and logged during drilling. Non-native,
odourous fill sands were encountered overlying silty clays within the former UST nest. BH19-2
and BH19-3 were characterized by a layer of topsoil overlying permeable course sand with trace
silts, and at depth silty clays. Bedrock was inferred at these locations at 2.4 to 3.0 m. Borehole
logs are available in Appendix B.

Groundwater was not encountered during drilling; however, the groundwater table was measured
between 1.60 and 1.93 m bgs upon stabilization of the well.

Total Volatile Organic Compound (tVOC) head-space readings were taken for the soil samples
prior to selection for submission of analyses to the laboratory. The handheld MiniRae 3000 Photo
lonization Detector (PID), measured from 6.5 to 15.7 ppm tVOC across all soil samples collected.

7.0 DISCUSSION

Soil samples from the tank nest (19-1), and groundwater from the on-Site well (19-2) were
collected as part of this Stage 2 PSI to investigate the presence or absence of PCOCs related to
the two APECs identified in the Stage 1 PSI. A summary of the findings for each APEC is
presented below.

APEC1 — Former Residential Heating Oil UST

Field observations from the drilling program demonstrated olfactory presence of hydrocarbons
within the fill sands of the former UST nest. The soil samples were pre-screened in the field, and

in the analyzed soil sample demonstrated detectable EPH and PAH’s, however each parameter

may not be suitable for relocation due to visual and olfactory concerns.

APEC2 — Off-Site Schedule 2 Activities - Auto Repair and Servicing Station

Analysis of groundwater from the well at 19-2, placed within the northeastern corner of the Site,
nearest to the off-Site APEC, initially demonstrated detectable levels of EPH’s and PAH’s,
including on exceedance of the parameter LEPHw (3,530 p/L) for protection of Aquatic Marine
Life (500 pg/L). Sample MW1-0219 was repeated at the laboratory, returning similar results.
However, after groundwater purging and sampling was repeated on March 11", 2019, non-
detectable results of LEPHw and PAHs were returned. In order to confirm the first groundwater
sample was false, a third purging and sampling event was completed March 20", 2019 with
repeated non-detectable results. Based on the data from the two follow up sampling events,
groundwater is not considered an issue at location 19-2.

The soil vapour probe installed at 19-3 was found to contain vacuum conditions due to an elevated
groundwater table, and therefore was not available for testing within the timeframe of this report.

The analytical results, in conjunction with the field observations indicate that there are no on-Site
concerns for PCOCs related to off-Site APEC2.

The following section displays the quality control (QC) data that is associated with your sample data. Groups of samples are prepared
in “batches” and analyzed in conjunction with QC samples that ensure your data is of the highest quality. Common QC types include:

+ Method Blank (Blk): A blank sample that undergoes sample processing identical to that carried out for the test samples. Method
blank results are used to assess contamination from the laboratory environment and reagents.

+ Duplicate (Dup): An additional or second portion of a randomly selected sample in the analytical run carried through the entire
analytical process. Duplicates provide a measure of the analytical method's precision (reproducibility).

+ Blank Spike (BS): A sample of known concentration which undergoes processing identical to that carried out for test samples, also
referred to as a laboratory control sample (LCS). Blank spikes provide a measure of the analytical method's accuracy.

+ Matrix Spike (MS): A second aliquot of sample is fortified with with a known concentration of target analytes and carried through
the entire analytical process. Matrix spikes evaluate potential matrix effects that may affect the analyte recovery.

+ Reference Material (SRM): A homogenous material of similar matrix to the samples, certified for the parameter(s) listed.
Reference Materials ensure that the analytical process 1s adequate to achieve acceptable recoveries of the parameter(s) tested.

Each QC type is analyzed at a 5-10% frequency, 1.e. one blank/duplicate/spike for every 10-20 samples. For all types of QC, the
specified recovery (% Rec) and relative percent difference (RPD) limits are derived from long-term method performance averages
and/or prescribed by the reference method.

The following section displays the quality control (QC) data that 1s associated with your sample data. Groups of samples are prepared
in “batches” and analyzed in conjunction with QC samples that ensure your data is of the highest quality Common QC types include

+ Method Blank (Blk): A blank sample that undergoes sample processing identical to that carried out for the test samples Method
blank results are used to assess contamination from the laboratory environment and reagents

+ Duplicate (Dup): An additional or second portion of a randomly selected sample in the analytical run carried through the entire
analytical process. Duplicates provide a measure of the analytical method's precision (reproducibllity)..

+ Blank Spike (BS): A sample of known concentration which undergoes processing identical to that carried out for test samples, also
referred to as a laboratory control sample (LCS). Blank spikes provide a measure of the analytical method's accuracy

+ Matrix Spike (MS): A second aliquot of sample 1s fortified with with a known concentration of target analytes and carried through
the entire analytical process. Matrix spikes evaluate potential matrix effects that may affect the analyte recovery.

+ Reference Material (SRM): A homogenous material of similar matrix to the samples, certified for the parameter(s) listed.
Reference Materials ensure that the analytical process 1s adequate to achieve acceptable recoveries of the parameter(s) tested.

Each QC type is analyzed at a 5-10% frequency, 1.e. one blank/duplicate/spike for every 10-20 samples For all types of QC, the

The following section displays the quality control (QC) data that 1s associated with your sample data. Groups of samples are prepared
in “batches” and analyzed in conjunction with QC samples that ensure your data is of the highest quality. Common QC types include:

+ Method Blank (Blk): A blank sample that undergoes sample processing identical to that carried out for the test samples. Method
blank results are used to assess contamination from the laboratory environment and reagents.

+ Duplicate (Dup): An additional or second portion of a randomly selected sample in the analytical run carried through the entire
analytical process. Duplicates provide a measure of the analytical method's precision (reproducibility).

+ Blank Spike (BS): A sample of known concentration which undergoes processing identical to that carried out for test samples, also
referred to as a laboratory control sample (LCS). Blank spikes provide a measure of the analytical method's accuracy

+ Matrix Spike (MS): A second aliquot of sample is fortified with with a known concentration of target analytes and carried through
the entire analytical process. Matrix spikes evaluate potential matrix effects that may affect the analyte recovery.

+ Reference Material (SRM): A homogenous material of similar matrix to the samples, certified for the parameter(s) listed.
Reference Materials ensure that the analytical process is adequate to achieve acceptable recoveries of the parameter(s) tested.

Each QC type is analyzed at a 5-10% frequency, i.e. one blank/duplicate/spike for every 10-20 samples. For all types of QC, the
specified recovery (% Rec) and relative percent difference (RPD) limits are derived from long-term method performance averages
and/or prescribed by the reference method

in “batches” and analyzed in conjunction with QC samples that ensure your data is of the highest quality. Common QC types include:

+ Method Blank (Blk): A blank sample that undergoes sample processing identical to that carried out for the test samples. Method
blank results are used to assess contamination from the laboratory environment and reagents.

+ Duplicate (Dup): An additional or second portion of a randomly selected sample in the analytical run carried through the entire
analytical process. Duplicates provide a measure of the analytical method's precision (reproducibility).

+ Blank Spike (BS): A sample of known concentration which undergoes processing identical to that carried out for test samples, also
referred to as a laboratory control sample (LCS). Blank spikes provide a measure of the analytical method's accuracy

+ Matrix Spike (MS): A second aliquot of sample is fortified with with a known concentration of target analytes and carried through
the entire analytical process. Matrix spikes evaluate potential matrix effects that may affect the analyte recovery.

+ Reference Material (SRM): A homogenous material of similar matrix to the samples, certified for the parameter(s) listed.
Reference Materials ensure that the analytical process is adequate to achieve acceptable recoveries of the parameter(s) tested.

Each QC type is analyzed at a 5-10% frequency, i.e. one blank/duplicate/spike for every 10-20 samples. For all types of QC, the
specified recovery (% Rec) and relative percent difference (RPD) limits are derived from long-term method performance averages
